summary: The confession becomes a contract. The princes, Levites, and priests 'set their seal' to a written covenant — eighty-plus names are listed — and the rest of the people bind themselves under curse and oath. The promises are concrete: no intermarriage with the peoples, no buying on the Sabbath, a yearly third of a didrachm for the temple, wood lots for the altar, firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes — 'we will not forsake the house of our God.'
whyItMatters: Revival here gets signatures. Every promise answers a failure named in chapter 19's history or chapter 23's relapse — this is what repentance looks like when it grows up: specific, written, witnessed, and funded.

keyVerses.text: And in regard to all these circumstances we make a covenant, and write it, and our princes, our Levites, and our priests, set their seal to it.
keyVerses.why: Confession becomes legislation — with names attached.

keyVerses.text: And that we will not, they said, give our daughters to the people of the land, nor will we take their daughters to our sons.
keyVerses.why: The first stipulation targets the community's most repeated failure — the drift that Solomon himself fell into.

keyVerses.text: And as for the people of the land who bring wares and all manner of merchandise to sell on the sabbath-day, we will not buy of them on the sabbath or on the holy day.
keyVerses.why: Sabbath-keeping by consumer decision — the buyer, not just the seller, bears the rule.

keyVerses.text: For the children of Israel and the children of Levi shall bring into the treasuries the first-fruits of the corn, and wine, and oil; and there are the holy vessels, and the priests, and the ministers, and the porters, and the singers: and we will not forsake the house of our God.
keyVerses.why: The covenant's last line is a vow of presence: the temple will not be abandoned again.

questions.question: Why sign and seal a document? Isn't a promise enough?
questions.answer: This community had just prayed through four centuries of broken promises. Writing, sealing, and naming signatories made the commitment public, permanent, and accountable — the same logic as a modern constitution. When failure came (chapter 23), there was a standard to appeal to.

questions.question: Why do the marriage rules come first?
questions.answer: Because 'the holy seed' (Ezra 9:2) was the covenant's future. Most readers see the issue as allegiance rather than ethnicity, though some scholars read ethnic exclusivism here too — marriages to the peoples of the land had repeatedly pulled Israel's kings and people into idolatry. The oath answers the exact drift the prayer of chapter 19 confessed.

questions.question: What is the third part of a didrachm?
questions.answer: A yearly temple tax. Exodus 30:13 set a half-shekel for the sanctuary; in Greek coinage that came to about a third of a didrachm. The community taxed itself voluntarily to keep the sacrifices burning — worship with a budget line.

questions.question: Why does wood delivery need a lottery system?
questions.answer: The altar never went out, and Jerusalem's hills were not thick with forest. Lots assigned each family's turn to bring wood yearly — 'according to the house of our families, at certain set times' — so the fire on the altar never depended on someone's mood.

questions.question: Is this covenant legalism?
questions.answer: Read the order: chapter 18 is the word received with joy, chapter 19 is confession, chapter 20 is response. Obedience here is the fruit of mercy remembered, not the price of it — the shape Paul later calls faith working through love. The failure mode appears in chapter 23, and it is drift, not decree.
